summary: Defines the Simple Public-Key Mechanism, a way for programs using the Generic Security Service API to authenticate each other and protect messages using public-key cryptography.

eli5.summary: Two people use a public lock and a private key to prove who they are and keep notes secret. This is a recipe for programs to do the same.

questions: what is the difference between spkm-1 and spkm-2
how does spkm authenticate with public keys
what is quality of protection in gss-api
subtitle: A public-key mechanism for GSS-API: sign-in, key setup and message protection using certificates instead of shared secrets.

tldr.problem: Applications that use the Generic Security Service API needed a mechanism built on public keys rather than the symmetric keys of Kerberos, including real digital signatures and no need for secure clocks.
tldr.mechanism: SPKM defines two GSS-API mechanisms, SPKM-1 (random numbers) and SPKM-2 (timestamps), with ASN.1 tokens that authenticate the peers, negotiate algorithms, establish a context key and protect each message.
tldr.outcome: Applications that already call GSS-API can use it as a drop-in replacement for Kerberos, with optional non-repudiable signatures on messages.

today: RFC 2025 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 1508 and RFC 1509 for the GSS-API itself.

sections.title: Why a Public-Key GSS-API Mechanism
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service API (GSS-API) lets an application ask for authentication, integrity and confidentiality without knowing which security technology does the work. A document that defines the token formats and procedures for one such technology is called a mechanism. SPKM is one, and it is built on a public-key infrastructure.

The Background section explains why. The Kerberos Version 5 mechanism (RFC 1964) is well established, but some applications need a mechanism based on public keys. SPKM promises four things: unilateral and mutual authentication without secure timestamps, algorithm identifiers so algorithms can change, true digital signatures (supporting non-repudiation) as an option for signing and sealing messages, and data formats that stay close to the Kerberos mechanism for easy implementation. Because it follows the interface of RFC 1508, it can replace Kerberos in any application that calls GSS-API.

The RFC defines two mechanisms. SPKM-1 uses random numbers for replay detection while the context is set up. SPKM-2 requires secure timestamps for that purpose. The object identifiers are {spkm spkm-1(1)} and {spkm spkm-2(2)}.
sections.eli5: Some programs want to prove who they are with public locks and private keys instead of a shared password. SPKM lets them do that using the same plug as the older Kerberos way.

sections.title: The Four Kinds of Algorithm
sections.content:
SPKM names four algorithm roles, each picked by identifier so new algorithms can be added later. Only some are MANDATORY, and some are RECOMMENDED; the rest are optional. Confidentiality is not mandatory, since that could make the implementation impossible to export.

  • I-ALG (integrity): checks that a message was not altered. md5WithRSAEncryption is MANDATORY: an RSA signature on the MD5 hash, giving integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation. DES-MAC is RECOMMENDED. md5-DES-CBC and sum64-DES-CBC are also described.
  • C-ALG (confidentiality): a symmetric cipher for encrypting data. DES-CBC is RECOMMENDED.
  • K-ALG (key establishment): sets up the shared context key inside the authentication exchange. RSAEncryption is MANDATORY: the initiator makes the key and encrypts it with the target's RSA public key. id-rsa-key-transport and dhKeyAgreement (Diffie-Hellman, which needs a reply from the target) are other examples.
  • O-ALG (one-way function): derives subkeys from the context key. MD5 is MANDATORY; SHA is another example.

A subkey of k bits is the rightmost k bits of OWF(context_key || x || n || s || context_key). Here x is the ASCII character C (confidentiality) or I (keyed integrity), n is the number of the algorithm in the agreed list, and s is a stage counter that starts at the character 0. This keeps the encryption key and the integrity key different.
sections.eli5: SPKM lets the two sides choose from a menu of ways to sign, scramble, share a secret and make new keys. A few choices are required so that everyone has at least one in common.

sections.title: Negotiating Algorithms
sections.content:
In the first context token the initiator offers an ordered list of confidentiality algorithms and an ordered list of integrity algorithms. The target answers by returning the subset it supports, in the same relative order. The first algorithm of each agreed list becomes the default for the context.

For key establishment the initiator offers a set of K-ALGs, plus the key (or key half) for its preferred first choice. If the target dislikes that one it picks another from the set and sends its own key material with the choice; otherwise it sends a delete token and the context is never established. If the target picks a two-pass algorithm such as dhKeyAgreement, the initiator sends its key half in a further reply. The initiator also offers O-ALGs, and the one the target picks is used for subkey derivation.

When no response is expected (unilateral authentication in SPKM-2), the initiator's offered algorithms are simply the ones used, and the target must send a delete token if that is unacceptable.
sections.eli5: One side shows a list of choices in order of preference. The other side crosses out the ones it cannot do, and they use the first one left.

sections.title: Setting Up a Security Context
sections.content:
All tokens are wrapped in the GSS-API framing, InitialContextToken, naming SPKM-1 or SPKM-2, and encoded with ASN.1 BER restricted to the DER subset. Context setup uses three token types: SPKM-REQ (initiator to target), SPKM-REP-TI (target to initiator) and SPKM-REP-IT (initiator to target), plus SPKM-ERROR.

Which tokens flow depends on the mechanism and on whether mutual authentication was requested. SPKM-2 unilateral needs only SPKM-REQ, which authenticates the initiator to the target. SPKM-1 unilateral uses SPKM-REQ and SPKM-REP-TI, which authenticates the target to the initiator. Mutual authentication with SPKM-2 uses REQ and REP-TI, while SPKM-1 adds a third token, REP-IT. The RFC says typical use is expected to be mutual authentication and that unilateral authentication is not generally recommended.

The REQ token carries a token id, a context-id, protocol version bits, an optional timestamp (mandatory for SPKM-2), random numbers, the target and source names, the context data and the key establishment material. Its integrity field is normally a digital signature, but it can be a MAC, for example if the initiator wants to remain anonymous or a cached context is being re-established. Certificates can travel in the first token, come back in the reply if the initiator sets the target-certif-data-required option, or be obtained locally.

An error in REQ or REP-TI causes an SPKM-ERROR token. The RFC also describes using it to settle RSA modulus length: the initiator signs with the strongest RSA it supports, and if the target cannot verify it, the target replies with an error token signed with a shorter one.
sections.eli5: Setting up is like a secret handshake. One side sends a signed hello, the other signs a reply, and sometimes the first side signs once more. If something is wrong, an error note is sent.

sections.title: Protecting Messages and Ending the Context
sections.content:
After setup, the application calls gss_getMIC() to get a separate integrity token or gss_wrap() to get a token that holds the data, optionally encrypted. The SPKM-MIC and SPKM-WRAP tokens each begin with a header holding a token id, the context-id, optional algorithm indicators and an optional sequence number. The checksum is computed over the header followed by the data, which binds the data to the header and makes splicing harder. For SPKM the word checksum covers signatures, hashes and MACs alike.

For encryption, an 8-byte random confounder is put in front of the data because the CBC initialization vector is zero. With md5-DES-CBC and DES-CBC, the MD5 hash is appended to the padded data and everything is encrypted in one pass. sum64-DES-CBC requires that confidentiality be requested; otherwise SPKM returns an error.

Sequence numbers are used purely for security, to catch malicious loss, replay or reordering, and the RFC recommends that applications request sequencing and replay detection. The number is four bytes with a direction indicator (FALSE for the initiator, TRUE for the acceptor). A higher than expected number yields GSS_S_GAP_TOKEN, and a lower one yields a duplicate, unsequenced or old token status. A wrong direction yields GSS_S_UNSEQ_TOKEN.

The SPKM-DEL token deletes a context. It is built like a MIC token with zero-length data, and an invalid one leaves the context in place.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a sealed wrapper with a counter on it, so a spy cannot copy an old message, drop one or swap the order without being noticed.

sections.title: Quality of Protection and Status Codes
sections.content:
The Quality of Protection (QOP) parameter lets a caller choose which agreed algorithm protects a message. It is a 32-bit unsigned integer split into two 16-bit halves, one for confidentiality and one for integrity. Each half has a 5-bit Type Specifier (TS), a 3-bit unspecified field (U), a 4-bit implementation-specific field (IA) and a 4-bit mechanism-defined field (MA).

A receiver reads MA first. If it is zero it reads IA, and if that is also zero it uses TS. A TS of zero means the default algorithm for the context. TS values are portable across mechanisms. For confidentiality they mean strong, medium or weak, where weak is an effective key length of 40 bits or less and strong is 80 bits or more. For integrity they mean non-repudiation supported or repudiable. The MA values for SPKM are 1 for DES-CBC (confidentiality) and 1 and 2 for md5WithRSA and DES-MAC (integrity).

The initiator's integrity list must contain at least one non-repudiable digital signature algorithm and at least one other, repudiable one, and so must the target's returned list. This guarantees that every implementation offers both kinds. The RFC also lists symbolic minor status codes, such as GSS_SPKM_S_SG_CONTEXT_DELETED, so implementations report the same errors.
sections.eli5: A message can ask for a quality level, like strong or weak scrambling, instead of naming an exact method, and the mechanism picks one that fits.

sections.title: Parsing Tokens and Context IDs
sections.content:
Every SPKM implementation must provide a support function, SPKM_Parse_token. It takes a token and reports the mechanism, the token type and the context handle, without doing any cryptographic checks. An application with several contexts open can use it to decide which GSS function and which context to use for an incoming token. Use of the function is optional for applications. The token types are numbered 1 through 6: init, accept, error, sign (getMIC), seal (wrap) and delete.

The context-id in each token is a random number that must be fresh, but need not be unpredictable. The initiator supplies the first part and, when a reply is expected, the target adds its own, so both sides contribute to freshness and tokens from an old context cannot be replayed into a new one. In SPKM-2 unilateral authentication the target contributes nothing, so the key-src-bind field is required to help it trust the freshness of the token.

The section on name types says that no mandatory name forms have yet been defined. Optional ones are a user name, a machine UID and a string UID.
sections.eli5: Each conversation gets a ticket number made from a random piece from both sides. The helper tool just reads the label on a message to say what kind it is and which conversation it belongs to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are discussed throughout the memo. In practice that means the security reasoning sits in the design itself: the confounder, the header-bound checksums, the sequence numbers and direction indicator against reflection, the shared contribution to the context-id, and the signed or MACed context tokens.

The RFC also notes weaknesses of individual algorithms. Without the confounder, the strength of md5-DES-CBC is at most that of DES under a known-plaintext attack. For sum64-DES-CBC, encryption is a requirement for the integrity to be secure.
sections.eli5: The safety tricks are built into every step, like counters, random pieces and signatures, instead of in one separate chapter.
